summary: Proposes Limited Transmit, a TCP tweak that sends new data after the first duplicate acknowledgments. This helps recover from loss without waiting for a timeout, especially when the congestion window is small. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: When a packet goes missing, TCP normally waits either for three identical acknowledgments or for a timeout of at least a second. This RFC makes the sender answer the first two identical acknowledgments by sending a little more data, which often produces the third acknowledgment that triggers the fast repair.

subtitle: Send new data on the first two duplicate ACKs, so a lost segment is found by fast retransmit instead of a slow timeout.

tldr.problem: TCP only resends a lost segment quickly when three duplicate acknowledgments arrive, so a connection with a small congestion window often waits for a retransmission timeout instead, and the minimum timeout is a whole second.
tldr.mechanism: Limited Transmit tells the sender to send new data on the first two consecutive duplicate acknowledgments, as long as the receiver's window allows it and no more than two segments beyond the congestion window are outstanding.
tldr.outcome: The extra acknowledgments usually supply the third duplicate acknowledgment that Fast Retransmit needs, so the loss is repaired without waiting for the timer.

today: RFC 3042 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It describes a change to TCP senders, and the RFC says it is implemented in the ns network simulator, where the mechanism can be enabled for a connection with the option named singledup_.

sections.title: Why TCP Recovers Slowly
sections.content:
TCP's loss recovery does not work well when the congestion window at the sender is small. That happens when there is only a limited amount of data to send, when the receiver-advertised window limits it, or when end-to-end congestion control constrains a connection with a small bandwidth-delay product.

TCP has two ways to recover from a missing segment. The first is the retransmission timeout: if an acknowledgment for a segment does not arrive within a certain time, the segment is resent. The second is Fast Retransmit, which resends a segment when three duplicate acknowledgments arrive at the sender. Duplicate acknowledgments are also triggered by packet reordering in the Internet, so the sender waits for three of them to tell loss and reordering apart. Once in a loss recovery phase, the segment can be resent using slow start-based recovery, Fast Recovery, NewReno, or loss recovery based on selective acknowledgments.

The retransmission timeout is based on measured round-trip times, and to avoid resending segments that are only delayed rather than lost, the minimum timeout is conservatively chosen to be 1 second. So it pays to detect and recover from as many losses as possible without waiting for a long timeout, particularly when the connection is idle. But if not enough duplicate acknowledgments arrive, Fast Retransmit is never triggered, which happens when the congestion window is small or when many segments in a window are lost. With a congestion window of three segments, one dropped segment produces at most two duplicate acknowledgments, and since three are needed, a timeout is required to resend the dropped packet.

The RFC cites a study in which roughly 56% of the retransmissions sent by a busy web server were sent after the timeout expired, while only 44% were handled by Fast Retransmit, and in which only 4% of the timeout-based retransmissions could have been avoided with SACK. Using the technique in this document, 25% of those timeout-based retransmissions would likely have been avoided.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP normally waits for three identical acknowledgments before it resends a lost packet, and otherwise it waits for a timeout of at least a second. When the amount of data in flight is small, only one or two identical acknowledgments arrive, so the sender ends up waiting for the timer instead.

sections.title: The Limited Transmit Algorithm
sections.content:
When a TCP sender has previously unsent data queued for transmission, it should use the Limited Transmit algorithm, which calls for the sender to transmit new data upon the arrival of the first two consecutive duplicate acknowledgments, provided two conditions hold.

The first condition is that the receiver's advertised window allows the transmission of the segment. The second is that the amount of outstanding data would remain less than or equal to the congestion window plus 2 segments. In other words, the sender may send at most two segments beyond the congestion window.

The congestion window must not be changed when these new segments are transmitted. Assuming that the new segments and the corresponding acknowledgments are not dropped, the procedure allows the sender to infer loss using the standard Fast Retransmit threshold of three duplicate acknowledgments. This is more robust to reordered packets than retransmitting an old packet on the first or second duplicate acknowledgment would be.

One restriction comes with selective acknowledgments. If the connection is using SACK, the data sender must not send new segments in response to duplicate acknowledgments that carry no new SACK information, because a misbehaving receiver can generate such acknowledgments to trigger inappropriate transmission of data segments.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule is short. When a duplicate acknowledgment arrives, the sender may put one more new segment on the wire, but only if the receiver has room for it and only if the connection is not already two segments over its limit. The congestion window itself does not move.

sections.title: Why This Does Not Break Congestion Control
sections.content:
Limited Transmit follows the conservation of packets principle of congestion control. Each of the first two duplicate acknowledgments indicates that a segment has left the network, and the sender has not yet decided that a segment has been dropped, so it has no reason to believe that the current congestion control state is inaccurate. Sending segments in this situation therefore does not deviate from the spirit of TCP's congestion control principles.

Packet reordering is not a rare network event, and the earlier TCP specification, RFC 2581, provides no way to send data on the first two duplicate acknowledgments that arrive at the sender. That causes a burst of segments to be sent when an acknowledgment for new data does arrive after a reordering. With Limited Transmit, data packets are clocked out by incoming acknowledgments, so the transmission is not as bursty.

The algorithm is implemented in the ns network simulator, where it can be enabled for a given TCP connection with the option named singledup_.
sections.plainLanguage: Each duplicate acknowledgment tells the sender that a packet did get through, so the network is not obviously congested and sending two more packets is fair. Sending them one at a time as the acknowledgments arrive also spreads the traffic out, instead of releasing a burst later.

sections.title: Related Work: ECN and Rate Halving
sections.content:
Deployment of Explicit Congestion Notification may benefit connections with small congestion windows. ECN gives a way of indicating congestion to the end host without dropping segments, so a sender can avoid many of the Fast Retransmits and retransmission timeouts that would otherwise be needed to detect dropped segments.

The RFC notes that when ECN-enabled TCP traffic competes with traffic that does not use ECN, the ECN-enabled traffic can receive up to 30% higher goodput. For bulk transfers the relative benefit of ECN is greatest when, on average, each flow has 3-4 outstanding packets during each round-trip time. The RFC uses this as an estimate of the performance impact of a flow using Limited Transmit, since both ECN and Limited Transmit reduce the reliance on the retransmission timer for signalling congestion.

The Rate-Halving congestion control algorithm uses a form of limited transmit, calling for a data segment to be transmitted on every second duplicate acknowledgment that arrives at the sender. That algorithm decouples the decision of what to send from the decision of when to send it. However, like Limited Transmit, it always sends a new data segment on the second duplicate acknowledgment.
sections.plainLanguage: Two other pieces of work touch on the same idea. ECN lets a network signal congestion instead of dropping packets, and a related algorithm called Rate Halving also sends a new segment on the second duplicate acknowledgment.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC judges the extra security implications of the change to be minimal compared with TCP's existing weaknesses. The concern is the subversion of end-to-end congestion control by false duplicate acknowledgments, where a false duplicate acknowledgment is one that does not actually acknowledge new data received at the receiver. False duplicate acknowledgments could come from duplicate acknowledgments that are themselves duplicated in the network, or from misbehaving receivers that send them on purpose.

When the receiver has agreed to use SACK, the sender has fairly strong protection. A duplicate acknowledgment that acknowledges new data reports the sequence numbers of that new data, so the sender can check that an arriving duplicate acknowledgment acknowledges data it has actually sent and for which no previous acknowledgment has been received, before sending new data in response. For further protection the sender could keep a record of packet boundaries for transmitted data packets and recognise at most one valid acknowledgment for each packet.

Some limited protection is possible without SACK, by keeping a record of the number of packets transmitted and recognising at most one acknowledgment per packet as a trigger for sending new data, but that accounting would need extra state and complexity at the sender and does not seem necessary.

The most important protection comes from the limited potential of duplicate acknowledgments to subvert congestion control. When the sender receives fewer duplicate acknowledgments than the threshold, a misbehaving receiver might send two duplicate acknowledgments after each regular acknowledgment, and one might imagine the sender then sending at three times its allowed rate. With Limited Transmit the sender may only exceed the congestion window by less than the duplicate acknowledgment threshold of three segments, so it would not send a new packet for each duplicate acknowledgment received. When the sender receives at least a threshold number of duplicate acknowledgments, a TCP with Limited Transmit behaves essentially the same as one without it: the congestion window is halved and a loss recovery period is started.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone on the path could send fake duplicate acknowledgments to make the sender send more than it should. The RFC argues that the rule limits how much that helps an attacker, because the sender may only go two segments beyond its window and cannot send a packet for every fake acknowledgment it receives.

items.title: Room in the window
items.text: The receiver's advertised window must allow the segment.

items.title: Two segments of slack
items.text: Outstanding data must stay within the congestion window plus 2 segments.

items.title: The window does not move
items.text: The congestion window must not be changed when the new segments are sent.

items.title: Not with SACK
items.text: With SACK in use, no new data is sent for a duplicate ACK carrying no new SACK information.
